Welcome to the Vault

Hi, and welcome to the Vault.

This is not a diet. There are no meal plans you will quit by Thursday, no "never eat carbs again" rules, and no starving. The Skinny Laws are small, sneaky changes that make being lean feel easy and normal. Stack a few of them and your body stops fighting you.

There are 120 hacks inside, split into 12 Laws. You don't need all of them. Most people find 5 to 10 that fit their life, and that is enough to change everything.

Tap the menu at any time to jump to a section. Tick "I tried this" on the hacks you test, and your progress saves on this device.

How to use it

1
Take the 60-second quiz

Find your eating type. It tells you which Laws to read first.

2
Pick 3 hacks only

Start small. Three hacks you actually do beat thirty you read about.

3
Do the 30-Day Challenge

One tiny action a day. By day 30 the Laws run on autopilot.

4
Come back when you get stuck

Use search or the tag filters to find the right hack for the problem you have today.

What's your eating type?

Answer 5 quick questions. Pick the answer that sounds most like you. No wrong answers.

1. When do you usually eat more than you meant to?
2. What is most often in your hand?
3. How does your breakfast usually look?
4. Finish the sentence: "I'd be lean if only..."
5. After you overeat, you usually feel...
Law 01 of 12 🍽️

The Hunger Laws

Turn hunger down instead of fighting it

“You don't beat hunger with willpower. You turn the volume down.”

Here is the secret nobody tells you: lean people are not stronger than you. They are just less hungry. Their meals are built to switch hunger off, so they don't spend all day fighting it.

Hunger is not your enemy. It is a signal. And signals can be turned up or turned down by what you eat, what order you eat it in, and how fast you eat it.

This chapter gives you 10 ways to turn that volume down. No starving. No 'just ignore it.' You will eat real, filling food and feel satisfied. That is the whole point.

In this Law: The Protein AnchorVeggies Go FirstThe Vinegar ShotThe Big Bowl TrickThe 20-Minute MealThe Hunger ScaleChew Your CaloriesThe Fiber StackThe Flavor FenceThe Real Food Default
#001HungerQuick wins

The Protein Anchor

Your body keeps you hungry until it gets enough protein. So give it protein first.

Build every meal around a palm-to-hand-sized serving of protein, and put it on the plate first. Aim for roughly 25 to 40 grams per meal. Breakfast matters most, because that is where most people eat almost none.

Why it works

Scientists call this 'protein leverage.' Researchers Simpson and Raubenheimer found that many animals, and likely humans, keep eating until they hit a protein target. If your food is low in protein, you keep eating to get there. Protein also takes more energy to digest and keeps you full longer than carbs or fat.

How to do it

  1. Pick your anchor for each meal: eggs, Greek yogurt, chicken, fish, tofu, cottage cheese, lean beef or lentils.
  2. Put the protein on the plate before anything else, then add the rest around it.
  3. Swap a toast-only or cereal-only breakfast for eggs plus toast, or Greek yogurt plus fruit.
  4. Check lunch and dinner tonight: if you can't point to the protein, add some.

Pro move: Keep 'emergency protein' ready: boiled eggs, yogurt cups or a rotisserie chicken in the fridge.

#002HungerQuick winsEating out

Veggies Go First

Same food, different order, calmer blood sugar. The order you eat in really matters.

Eat the vegetables on your plate first, then the protein, and save the bread, rice, pasta or potatoes for last. You don't eat less food. You just change the order.

Why it works

A 2015 study from Weill Cornell Medicine found that when people ate vegetables and protein before carbs, their blood sugar after the meal was much lower than when they ate the carbs first. Fiber and protein slow down how fast the carbs hit your blood. Smoother blood sugar often means fewer crashes and fewer 'I need a snack now' moments later.

How to do it

  1. Look at your plate and split it into three zones: veggies, protein, carbs.
  2. Eat most of the veggies first, then the protein.
  3. Eat the carbs last and slowly.
  4. At restaurants, order a side salad or veggie starter so the 'veggies first' part happens automatically.

Pro move: Can't wait for the carbs? Even 10 minutes between the veggies and the bread helps.

#003HungerDrinks

The Vinegar Shot

A splash of vinegar before your pasta night can soften the blood sugar spike.

Before a meal that is heavy in carbs, have 1 tablespoon of vinegar mixed into a big glass of water, or eat a salad with a vinegar dressing first. Apple cider vinegar or any vinegar works. Never drink it straight.

Why it works

Several small studies, including work by Carol Johnston at Arizona State University, found that vinegar with a carb meal can lower the blood sugar rise afterwards. The acetic acid seems to slow down how fast your stomach empties and how fast starch turns into sugar. It is not magic fat-burning. It is just a smoother ride after a big carb meal.

How to do it

  1. Mix 1 tablespoon of vinegar into a large glass of water.
  2. Drink it with a straw just before your meal to protect your teeth.
  3. Or start the meal with a salad dressed in oil and vinegar.
  4. Rinse your mouth with plain water afterwards.

Pro move: If you have reflux, stomach problems or take diabetes medicine, skip this or ask your doctor first.

#004HungerKitchen

The Big Bowl Trick

Eat a bigger plate of food for fewer calories. This is the loophole.

Fill your plate with foods that are heavy with water and fiber, like soup, veggies, berries and salad. They take up lots of room in your stomach but carry few calories. You get a big, satisfying portion without overdoing it.

Why it works

Barbara Rolls at Penn State spent years studying 'energy density,' which means calories per bite. Her research found that people tend to eat about the same weight of food each day. So when that food is full of water and fiber, you feel full on fewer calories. Her team also found that starting a meal with a broth-based soup or a big salad helped people eat less at the meal overall.

How to do it

  1. Add one extra cup of veggies to what you already eat: spinach in eggs, zucchini in pasta sauce, peppers in wraps.
  2. Swap half the rice or pasta for cauliflower rice or zucchini noodles.
  3. Start dinner with a cup of broth-based soup or a big side salad.
  4. Choose fresh fruit over dried fruit. Same sugar, way more volume.

Pro move: Mix 'half and half': half normal pasta, half veggie noodles. You barely notice the difference.

#005HungerMindsetQuick wins

The 20-Minute Meal

Your stomach sends the 'I'm full' message on a delay. Slow down and let it arrive.

Make every main meal last at least 20 minutes. Set a timer if you have to. Slow eating lets your fullness signal catch up with your fork.

Why it works

When food reaches your gut, it releases fullness hormones that tell your brain you have had enough. This takes time, often around 20 minutes. If you finish a plate in 7 minutes, your brain has not got the message yet, so you go back for more. Eat slowly and the message shows up while you are still eating.

How to do it

  1. Put your fork down between every bite.
  2. Chew each bite until it is soft, then swallow before picking the fork back up.
  3. Take a sip of water or say something to someone between bites.
  4. Set a 20-minute timer and try to still have food on your plate when it rings.

Pro move: Eat with your non-dominant hand or with chopsticks. It slows you down with zero effort.

#006HungerMindset

The Hunger Scale

Rate your hunger from 1 to 10 and you will never eat on autopilot again.

Before you eat, rate your hunger from 1 (starving and shaky) to 10 (painfully stuffed). Try to start eating at about a 3 or 4 and stop at about a 6 or 7. That is 'comfortably satisfied,' not stuffed.

Why it works

Most overeating happens because we don't check in. We eat because food is there or because the plate is not empty. A simple number makes you notice your body. Waiting until you are a 1 or 2 is also a trap, because being too hungry makes you eat fast and overshoot. So this hack is about eating when you are truly hungry, not waiting until you are starving.

How to do it

  1. Before each meal today, silently give yourself a number from 1 to 10.
  2. Halfway through the meal, pause and rate yourself again.
  3. When you hit 6 or 7, stop and wait 10 minutes. You can always have more if you are still hungry.
  4. If you often reach 1 or 2 during the day, add a snack with protein. Real hunger deserves food.

Pro move: Write your before and after numbers in your phone notes for 3 days. Patterns show up fast.

#007HungerDrinks

Chew Your Calories

A smoothie and a bowl of the same fruit do not fill you up the same way.

Get most of your calories from food you chew, not drinks. Swap juices, sweet coffees and big smoothies for whole food. If you love smoothies, make them thick and eat them from a bowl with a spoon.

Why it works

Drinks go down fast and skip a lot of the chewing and stomach stretch that tell your brain you are full. Studies comparing liquid and solid versions of similar calories often find that liquid calories are less filling, so people don't eat less later to make up for them. Chewing gives your body time and signals to register the food.

How to do it

  1. List every drink you had yesterday that was not water, tea or black coffee.
  2. Pick one to swap: orange juice becomes a whole orange, a sweet latte becomes a smaller or unsweetened one.
  3. If you keep your smoothie, make it thicker, add Greek yogurt for protein, and eat it with a spoon.
  4. Add toppings you have to chew, like berries or a few nuts.

Pro move: Order your coffee 'one size smaller.' You still get your ritual.

#008HungerBloat

The Fiber Stack

Fiber is the most underrated fullness tool in your kitchen. Stack it at every meal.

Add one high-fiber food to every meal. Think beans, lentils, chia seeds, oats, berries, pears, raspberries, broccoli or whole grains. Small add-ons count.

Why it works

Fiber slows down digestion, adds bulk and feeds the good bacteria in your gut. It keeps food in your stomach longer, so you stay full longer. Most people eat far less fiber than the recommended amount, so this is an easy win for almost everyone.

How to do it

  1. Stir 1 tablespoon of chia seeds or ground flax into yogurt or oats.
  2. Add half a can of rinsed beans or lentils to soups, salads or sauces.
  3. Pick raspberries or blackberries, some of the highest-fiber fruits.
  4. Increase fiber slowly over a week and drink more water, so your stomach can adjust.

Pro move: Going too fast with fiber can cause bloating. Add one new fiber food every few days.

#009HungerSocialEating out

The Flavor Fence

Buffets make you eat more because of variety. Use that same trick in reverse.

Keep main meals simple, with a few flavors. Too many different foods on the table makes you keep eating long after you are full. Save variety for your veggies, where more is actually good.

Why it works

This is called 'sensory-specific satiety,' studied by Barbara Rolls and others. You get tired of a flavor as you eat it, which helps you stop. But a new flavor 'resets' your appetite. That is why you always have room for dessert. Fewer flavors per meal helps your natural stop signal work.

How to do it

  1. Build meals with 1 protein, 1 or 2 veggies and 1 carb, instead of lots of little dishes.
  2. At parties and buffets, pick 3 foods you love most, instead of a bite of everything.
  3. Use variety on purpose with veggies: mix 3 or 4 colors in a salad to help you eat more of them.

Pro move: Snack boards with 8 kinds of crackers and cheese are appetite resets in disguise. Pick two.

#010HungerShopping

The Real Food Default

Ultra-processed food made people eat around 500 more calories a day. Without noticing.

Make most of your meals from foods that still look like where they came from: meat, fish, eggs, beans, veggies, fruit, potatoes, rice, oats. You don't need to be perfect. Just shift the balance.

Why it works

In a 2019 study at the US National Institutes of Health, Kevin Hall had people live in a lab and eat either an ultra-processed diet or a minimally processed one. They could eat as much as they wanted. On the ultra-processed diet, they ate about 500 more calories a day and gained weight. On the less processed diet, they ate less and lost weight, without trying.

How to do it

  1. Look at your 3 most common meals. Find the most processed part of each.
  2. Swap just that part: a packaged snack bar becomes fruit plus nuts, flavored instant oats become plain oats with berries.
  3. Aim for 'most meals real food,' not 'every bite perfect.'

Pro move: Quick rule: if it has a long ingredient list full of words you can't picture, it is probably ultra-processed.

Myth vs. Truth

Feeling hungry means your diet is working.

Constant hunger usually means your meals are missing protein, fiber or volume. Being hungry all day leads to overeating later, not to lasting results. The goal is to feel satisfied on nourishing food.

Tonight's Try-This

At dinner tonight, eat your veggies first, protein second and carbs last. Put your fork down between bites and make the meal last 20 minutes.

Journal prompts

What did I eat today that kept me full the longest?

When did I feel most hungry today, and what had I eaten before it?

What number on the hunger scale do I usually stop eating at?

“Hunger is a message, not an emergency. Feed it well and it goes quiet.”

— The Skinny Laws

The Kitchen Laws

Design your home so the lean choice is the lazy choice

“You don't rise to your willpower. You fall to your kitchen.”

You make hundreds of tiny food choices every day. Most of them you don't even notice. You grab what you see. You eat what is easy. You finish what is in front of you.

That sounds bad, but it is actually great news. If your choices are mostly automatic, you can change them by changing your space, not by trying harder.

This chapter is about setting up your kitchen so it works for you, even on your laziest, most tired day. Set it up once, and it keeps working while you sleep.

In this Law: The Invisible ShelfBowl It, Never Bag ItServe at the StoveThe Kitchen Closed RitualShop Fed, Shop ListedThe Eye-Level FridgeThe 20-Second RuleSunday Decision DayThe Clean Counter LawThe One Seat Rule
#011KitchenCravingsQuick wins

The Invisible Shelf

Out of sight really does mean out of mouth. Make your trigger foods boring to look at.

Move your trigger foods (the ones you can't stop eating once you start) into opaque containers or boxes, and put them on a high shelf or at the back of a cupboard. You are not banning them. You are just making them quiet.

Why it works

Seeing food is a strong cue to want food. Bright packaging is designed by experts to grab your attention. When you can't see the chips or cookies, you think about them less, so you eat them less often, without needing to fight yourself.

How to do it

  1. Pick your top 3 trigger foods.
  2. Put them in plain, non-see-through containers or a closed box labeled something boring like 'Misc.'
  3. Store them up high, down low or at the very back, anywhere but eye level.
  4. Put a healthy snack in the spot they used to be.

Pro move: Use clear containers for healthy food and opaque ones for treats. Let the good stuff be the pretty stuff.

#012KitchenQuick wins

Bowl It, Never Bag It

Eating from the bag has no bottom. A bowl does.

Never eat straight from a bag, box or tub. Always put a portion into a bowl or on a plate, close the package, and put it away before you take the first bite.

Why it works

A package gives you no stop signal. You keep reaching in until it is gone or you feel sick. A bowl gives your brain a clear end point. Putting the package away also adds a small step if you want more, which gives you time to ask if you are really still hungry.

How to do it

  1. Get out a small bowl every time you snack, even for a 'quick handful.'
  2. Pour your portion, then close the package and put it back in the cupboard.
  3. Sit down to eat it. No standing at the counter.
  4. If you still want more after, you can have more. Just repeat the whole process.

Pro move: Buy a set of small, pretty snack bowls. Make portioning feel like a treat, not a rule.

#013KitchenHungerSocial

Serve at the Stove

When the pot is on the table, seconds happen without you deciding.

Put food on plates in the kitchen and leave the pots and dishes on the stove. Bring only the plates to the table. Veggies and salad are the one exception: those can go on the table.

Why it works

When serving dishes sit in front of you, grabbing more is effortless and often automatic. When you have to get up and walk to the kitchen, you actually decide if you want more. Many times you won't, because the fullness signal has had time to arrive.

How to do it

  1. Tonight, plate everyone's food at the stove.
  2. Put a big bowl of salad or veggies on the table instead of the main dish.
  3. If you want seconds, wait 10 minutes first, then get up and serve yourself.

Pro move: Put leftovers into storage containers right after serving, before you sit down. No leftovers, no picking.

#014KitchenCravingsSleep

The Kitchen Closed Ritual

Restaurants close. Your kitchen can too. Give your evening a clear finish line.

After dinner, do a short 'closing' routine: clean up, wipe the counter, turn off the kitchen light and say (even just to yourself) 'kitchen closed.' It tells your brain that eating time is over for the day.

Why it works

A lot of extra eating happens at night out of habit, boredom or tiredness, not hunger. A ritual creates a clear line between 'eating time' and 'rest time.' Rituals are powerful because they turn a decision into a habit, so you don't have to fight yourself every night.

How to do it

  1. Right after dinner, put away all food and wipe the counters.
  2. Make a cup of herbal tea to take with you out of the kitchen.
  3. Turn off the kitchen light and leave the room.
  4. If you are truly hungry later, have a planned protein snack like Greek yogurt. Real hunger is allowed.

Pro move: Brush your teeth soon after dinner. Minty mouth plus a closed kitchen is a double lock.

#015ShoppingKitchen

Shop Fed, Shop Listed

A hungry brain in a grocery store is a salesperson's dream customer.

Only go food shopping after a meal, and always with a list. Stick to the list. Better yet, order groceries online, where you can't smell the bakery or see the checkout candy.

Why it works

When you are hungry, high-calorie food looks and smells more rewarding, so it is much easier to grab things you never planned to buy. Stores are also designed to make you buy on impulse. A full stomach and a list protect you from both.

How to do it

  1. Plan your shopping for right after breakfast, lunch or dinner.
  2. Write your list by store section so you can move fast.
  3. Shop the outer aisles first, where fresh food usually lives.
  4. Try online ordering for one week and notice how much less junk ends up in your cart.

Pro move: If a treat isn't on the list, it doesn't go in the cart. Decide at home, not in the aisle.

#016KitchenQuick winsShopping

The Eye-Level Fridge

Whatever you see first when you open the fridge is what you'll eat.

Wash and cut your fruit and veggies as soon as you get home, put them in clear containers and place them on the middle shelf, right at eye level. Move sauces, leftovers and treats lower or to the back.

Why it works

When you're hungry, you grab what is easy and ready. Whole, unwashed produce hidden in the crisper drawer loses to a ready-to-eat snack every time. Make the healthy choice the fastest one and you'll pick it without thinking.

How to do it

  1. Spend 20 minutes after shopping washing and cutting produce.
  2. Store it in clear containers on the middle shelf, front and center.
  3. Keep a ready-made dip nearby, like hummus or a Greek yogurt dip.
  4. Move treats and high-calorie leftovers to the bottom drawer or the back.

Pro move: Keep a bowl of washed fruit on the counter too. Make it the only food out in the open.

#017KitchenCravings

The 20-Second Rule

Add 20 seconds of hassle to a snack and you'll eat it far less often.

Add small bits of friction to the foods you overeat. Freeze them, wrap them tightly, store them in another room, or buy them only in single servings. Remove friction from healthy foods at the same time.

Why it works

Happiness researcher Shawn Achor wrote about this idea: small barriers of about 20 seconds are often enough to stop an automatic habit. You can still have the treat. But you have to want it, not just grab it on autopilot.

How to do it

  1. Put cookies or chocolate in the freezer, so you have to wait for them to soften.
  2. Store the chips in the garage, a high cupboard or a closed box.
  3. Buy treats in single-serving packs instead of family-sized bags.
  4. Do the opposite for healthy food: pre-cut, washed and in plain sight.

Pro move: Ask someone you live with to keep their snacks in their own drawer, out of your view.

#018KitchenShoppingMindset

Sunday Decision Day

Tired you makes bad food decisions. So let rested you decide in advance.

Once a week, plan your dinners and lunches for the week ahead and write them down. You're not deciding what to eat at 7pm when you're starving. You already decided on Sunday.

Why it works

By the end of a long day, your brain is tired of making choices. That is when takeout and snacking win. Deciding ahead of time removes the choice when you're weakest. Research on 'if-then' planning, led by psychologist Peter Gollwitzer, shows that deciding in advance makes people much more likely to follow through.

How to do it

  1. Every Sunday, write 5 dinners and 3 easy lunches for the week.
  2. Build your grocery list straight from that plan.
  3. Prep 1 or 2 things ahead: cook a batch of protein, chop veggies, make a big salad.
  4. Keep 2 'backup meals' you can make in 10 minutes for chaotic nights.

Pro move: Stick your meal plan on the fridge. Seeing it every day makes it feel like a promise.

#019KitchenQuick wins

The Clean Counter Law

Your counter is a billboard. Only let healthy food advertise there.

Clear every food off your kitchen counters except fruit and maybe a jar of nuts. No cereal boxes, no bread, no cookie jar, no candy dish.

Why it works

Food you see many times a day becomes food you eat many times a day. Each glance is a small nudge to eat. When the only thing in sight is fruit, the nudges push you in a good direction instead.

How to do it

  1. Walk into your kitchen now and look at every counter.
  2. Put all packaged food into cupboards.
  3. Place a bowl of fruit where the snacks used to be.
  4. Check the counters again every night as part of your kitchen-closed routine.

Pro move: Do the same in your car, desk and bag. Every place you spend time is a mini kitchen.

#020KitchenMindsetHunger

The One Seat Rule

If you eat everywhere, you'll want to eat everywhere. Give food one home.

Only eat sitting down at a table, with no phone, TV or laptop. No eating on the couch, in bed, standing in the kitchen or at your desk while working.

Why it works

A 2013 review in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, led by Eric Robinson, found that eating while distracted led people to eat more, both at that meal and later. When your attention is somewhere else, your brain doesn't fully register the food. Eating in the same spot also stops the couch and bed from becoming cues to snack.

How to do it

  1. Pick one spot in your home that is your eating spot.
  2. Put your phone in another room or face down during meals.
  3. If you want a snack while watching TV, put it in a bowl and eat it at the table first, then go back.
  4. At work, take your lunch away from your keyboard, even for 10 minutes.

Pro move: Set the table even when eating alone. It turns a meal into an event you actually notice.

Myth vs. Truth

People who stay lean just have more self-control around food.

Many lean people simply live in homes where tempting food is not always in sight or in reach. They make fewer hard choices because their space makes the easy choice the healthy one. You can build that same space.

Tonight's Try-This

Spend 10 minutes clearing your counters of everything except fruit, and move your top trigger food into an opaque container on a high shelf.

Journal prompts

What foods do I see the most in my kitchen, and are they helping me?

Where in my home do I usually eat without thinking?

What is one piece of friction I can add to my biggest trigger food?

“Stop fighting your kitchen. Redesign it, and let it fight for you.”

— The Skinny Laws

The Movement Laws

The lazy-girl way to burn more without living at the gym

“The gym is one hour. Your life is the other fifteen. Win the fifteen.”

Here is a secret the fitness world does not love to share: for most people, the gym is not the big lever. The big lever is all the small moving you do the rest of the day. Walking to the car. Pacing on a call. Carrying the laundry up the stairs. Scientists call it NEAT, which stands for non-exercise activity thermogenesis. You can just call it 'moving without trying'.

NEAT can change a lot from person to person, and from day to day. Lean people often are not training harder. They just sit less. They fidget, stand, walk and do stuff, without calling it a workout.

This chapter is the lazy-girl version of fitness. No punishing cardio. No 'burning off' last night's pizza. Just small, sneaky ways to move more that fit into the life you already have. Stack enough of them and your body quietly does the rest.

In this Law: The NEAT TakeoverThe 10-Minute Digestion WalkThe Walk-and-Talk LawThe Stair RuleStep SnacksThe Stand-to-Scroll RuleThe Habit HitchhikeThe Hungry Cardio TrapThe Far-Side Parking RuleThe Walking Pad Office
#021MovementQuick wins

The NEAT Takeover

Your daily steps can matter more than your workout. Here is how to use that.

Stop thinking of movement as 'the workout' and start thinking of it as your whole day. Find your current daily step average, then raise it slowly. Small, boring movement all day beats one hard session followed by 10 hours on the sofa.

Why it works

A well-known 1999 study in the journal Science, led by James Levine at the Mayo Clinic, overfed volunteers on purpose. The people who gained the least fat were the ones who naturally moved more in small ways, like fidgeting and standing. Daily movement adds up to far more than most people think, and it does not leave you wrecked or starving.

How to do it

  1. Check your phone or watch for your average steps over the last 7 days.
  2. Add 1,000 steps to that number. That is your new daily target for the next 2 weeks.
  3. Once it feels normal, add another 1,000. Keep going until you land around 7,000 to 10,000.

Pro move: Don't jump from 3,000 to 12,000 overnight. Slow raises stick. Big jumps burn you out by Thursday.

#022MovementCravingsQuick wins

The 10-Minute Digestion Walk

A short walk after eating can flatten your blood sugar spike. Timing is everything.

Within 30 minutes of finishing your biggest meal, go for an easy 10-minute walk. No sweat, no speed. Just a stroll around the block, the office or even your hallway.

Why it works

When you walk, your muscles pull sugar out of your blood to use as fuel. A 2022 review in the journal Sports Medicine found that even a few minutes of light walking after a meal lowered the blood sugar rise compared with sitting. Smaller spikes can mean fewer crashes and fewer 'I need something sweet' moments later.

How to do it

  1. Pick the meal you eat at home most often, usually dinner.
  2. Put your shoes by the door before you sit down to eat.
  3. When you finish, walk for 10 minutes before you touch the dishes or the couch.
  4. Can't go out? Walk laps of your home or up and down the stairs.

Pro move: Turn it into a ritual with your partner, kid or dog. Nobody skips a walk when the dog is staring at them.

#023MovementQuick wins

The Walk-and-Talk Law

Every phone call is a free walk you are currently wasting.

Make a rule: if you are on the phone and not looking at a screen, you are standing up and walking. Calls with mum, your best friend, customer service, voice notes. All of them are now walking time.

Why it works

Most of us spend hours a week on calls while sitting still. A 20-minute call at an easy pace can easily be 2,000 steps or more. You are doing the call anyway, so the steps cost you zero extra time.

How to do it

  1. Buy or dig out a pair of wireless earbuds so walking feels easy.
  2. The moment your phone rings, stand up before you answer.
  3. Pace your room, your hallway or walk outside for the whole call.
  4. For long work calls with no screen, book them as 'walking meetings' in your calendar.

Pro move: Stuck on hold with your bank? Perfect. That is the best cardio of your life.

#024MovementShape

The Stair Rule

Two floors or less? The lift is not for you anymore.

Set a simple, non-negotiable rule: if it is two floors or less, you take the stairs. Up or down. No debate, no 'just today'. Rules beat decisions because you don't have to think.

Why it works

Climbing stairs uses your biggest muscles, your glutes and thighs, so it takes much more effort than walking on flat ground. It is also great for shaping your legs and bum. And because it is a rule and not a choice, you never waste willpower arguing with yourself.

How to do it

  1. Decide your number right now: 'two floors or less, always stairs'.
  2. At home, stop leaving things at the bottom of the stairs to 'take up later'. Take each thing up now.
  3. At work or the mall, walk past the lift and look for the stair sign first.
  4. Once two floors is easy, make it three.

Pro move: Going up more than your rule? Take the stairs for the last two floors only. Still counts.

#025MovementCravingsQuick wins

Step Snacks

You snack on food all day. Start snacking on steps instead.

A step snack is a tiny burst of movement, 2 to 5 minutes, sprinkled through your day. Every hour or so, you get up and walk, do a lap, climb a flight of stairs or march on the spot. Small bites, big total.

Why it works

Long stretches of sitting keep your body in low-power mode. Short, regular breaks wake your muscles up and keep your daily movement ticking over. Ten step snacks of 3 minutes each is 30 minutes of walking, and you never had to 'find time'.

How to do it

  1. Set a quiet hourly reminder on your phone or watch from 9am to 5pm.
  2. When it buzzes, stand up and move for 2 to 5 minutes. Refill water, walk to the far bathroom, do one flight of stairs.
  3. Keep a tally on a sticky note. Aim for 8 step snacks a day.

Pro move: Feeling a craving? Take a step snack first. Often the craving was just boredom.

#026MovementMindsetQuick wins

The Stand-to-Scroll Rule

You are going to scroll anyway. Just don't do it sitting down.

Make one easy swap: when you open TikTok, Instagram or any feed just for fun, you stand up. Lean on the kitchen counter, pace, sway, stretch. Sitting is for work and meals. Scrolling is for standing.

Why it works

Standing uses more energy than sitting because your leg and core muscles have to work to keep you upright. It also makes you fidget and shift, which adds more small movement. And a nice bonus: you will probably scroll for less time, because standing gets boring faster than lying on the couch.

How to do it

  1. Tell yourself the rule out loud once: 'Scrolling is a standing activity'.
  2. Every time you catch yourself scrolling while sitting, stand up. No guilt, just stand.
  3. Add small moves while you stand: calf raises, side steps or gentle squats during videos.

Pro move: Watching this brand's videos? Do 10 calf raises per video. You're welcome.

#027MovementMindset

The Habit Hitchhike

Glue tiny moves onto things you already do every day, and they happen on autopilot.

Pick habits you never miss, like brushing your teeth, boiling the kettle or waiting for the microwave. Attach one tiny move to each one. The old habit becomes the trigger for the new one.

Why it works

New habits fail because you have to remember them. Habits you already have are automatic. When you hook a small move onto an automatic habit, you borrow its power. This is called habit stacking, and it works because the cue is already built into your day.

How to do it

  1. Write down 3 things you do every single day (for example: kettle, teeth, waiting for the shower to warm up).
  2. Match each one with a tiny move: 10 squats while the kettle boils, calf raises while you brush, 20 wall push-ups while the shower warms up.
  3. Use this sentence: 'After I ___, I will ___'. Stick it where the habit happens.

Pro move: Keep each move so small it feels silly. Silly and done beats impressive and skipped.

#028MovementHungerMindset

The Hungry Cardio Trap

If intense cardio makes you ravenous, it might be working against you.

Notice how you feel after long, hard cardio sessions. If you often want to eat the whole kitchen after, swap some of them for walking and strength training. Keep the moves that leave you feeling good, not starving.

Why it works

Hard cardio burns energy, but for some people it also turns hunger way up and makes the sofa feel extra tempting for the rest of the day. That can cancel out the effort. Walking barely touches your appetite, and strength training helps build muscle, which shapes your body and supports your metabolism.

How to do it

  1. For the next 2 weeks, rate your hunger from 1 to 10 about an hour after each workout.
  2. If hard cardio days are always a 8 or higher, swap 2 of those sessions for brisk walks.
  3. Add 2 short strength sessions a week, even 20 minutes of squats, lunges and push-ups at home.
  4. After any workout, eat a real meal with protein instead of 'rewarding' yourself with a treat.

Pro move: You don't need to 'earn' food with exercise, ever. Move to feel good, eat to fuel.

#029MovementQuick wins

The Far-Side Parking Rule

The best parking spot is the worst one. Seriously.

Stop circling for the closest spot. Park at the far end of the car park, get off the bus one stop early, or use the entrance that is furthest from where you need to go. Make distance the default.

Why it works

Each far-away choice adds a few hundred steps. Do it at work, the supermarket and school pick-up, and you can add thousands of steps a week without planning a single walk. Bonus: far spots are easier to find, so you stop wasting time and stress hunting for a space.

How to do it

  1. Today, park in the row furthest from the door. Every trip, every time.
  2. If you take the bus or train, get off one stop early on the way home at least 3 times a week.
  3. In big stores or malls, walk the long way round to the thing you need.

Pro move: Use a shopping basket instead of a trolley when you only need a few things. Carrying adds work, and you buy less junk.

#030MovementMaintenance

The Walking Pad Office

Turn boring screen time into free steps with one piece of kit.

A walking pad is a small, flat treadmill that slides under a standing desk or sits in front of your TV. You walk slowly, around 2 to 3 km per hour, while you answer emails, watch a show or scroll. Pair it with chores-as-movement on days you are home.

Why it works

You are not trying to sweat. You are replacing sitting time with gentle walking time. One hour at a slow pace can add several thousand steps. It is one of the easiest ways for people with desk jobs to move more without taking time away from anything.

How to do it

  1. Start with just 20 to 30 minutes a day at a slow speed. Slow is the whole point.
  2. Use it during low-focus tasks: emails, calls, Netflix, scrolling. Sit for deep work if you need to.
  3. No walking pad yet? Turn chores into movement instead: put on 3 songs and speed-clean, carry laundry one load at a time, hand-wash the car.

Pro move: Wear proper trainers on the pad, not socks or slippers. Your feet and knees will thank you.

Myth vs. Truth

If you don't sweat, it doesn't count.

Sweat is just how your body cools down. It is not a score. Gentle, all-day movement like walking and standing often adds up to more than one intense workout, and it doesn't make you ravenous afterwards.

Tonight's Try-This

After dinner tonight, put your shoes on and take a 10-minute walk before you touch the dishes or the sofa. Put on one podcast episode or call a friend and just go.

Journal prompts

What are 3 things I do every day that I could glue a tiny move onto?

When during my day do I sit the longest without getting up?

Which kind of movement leaves me feeling energised, and which leaves me starving?

“You don't need a harder workout. You need a less still life.”

— The Skinny Laws

Law 07 of 12 🛒

The Grocery & Prep Laws

Win the week at the store, not at 9pm in front of the fridge

“Whatever is in your kitchen is what you will eat. So choose it at the store.”

Here is a secret most diet plans skip. Most of your eating choices are made before you ever feel hungry. They are made in the grocery store, with a cart in your hand.

If chips are in the cupboard, you will eat chips. If ready-to-eat protein is in the fridge, you will eat protein. Your willpower at 9pm is tired. Your kitchen is not.

This chapter makes your kitchen do the hard work for you. Smarter lists, faster labels, lazy prep, and flavor tricks that make lean food taste like a treat. Less thinking. Less cooking. Better results.

In this Law: The Ring + Freezer RouteThe Frozen Veg StashThe 5-Second Protein TestThe Ready Protein RuleComponents, Not MealsThe Default Dinner RotationThe 3-Ingredient Protein PlateThe Portion Pack SundayThe Big Batch HourThe Flavor Cheat Shelf
#031ShoppingQuick wins

The Ring + Freezer Route

Shop in a U shape and your cart gets leaner without a single hard decision.

Walk the outer ring of the store first: produce, meat, fish, eggs, dairy. Then go straight to the frozen aisle for frozen veg, fruit and plain proteins. Only enter the middle aisles with a list, and only for the items on it.

Why it works

Stores put fresh, whole foods around the edges and the snacky, easy-to-overeat stuff in the middle. Every aisle you walk down is another chance for an impulse buy. Fewer aisles means fewer temptations, with zero willpower needed.

How to do it

  1. Start at produce and fill half your cart there.
  2. Hit the protein and dairy walls next.
  3. Go to the freezer section for bags of veg, fruit and plain shrimp or chicken.
  4. Enter a middle aisle only if an item on your list lives there, then walk out.

Pro move: Shop after a meal, never hungry. A full stomach writes a smarter cart.

#032KitchenShoppingHunger

The Frozen Veg Stash

The cheapest, fastest weight loss tool in the store is sitting in the freezer.

Keep at least 4 bags of frozen vegetables in your freezer at all times. Add a handful to almost every meal: eggs, pasta, rice, soup, even instant noodles. Frozen fruit goes into yogurt and oats.

Why it works

Frozen veg is picked and frozen fast, so it keeps its nutrients. It never goes bad, so there is no guilt and no waste. Veg adds lots of volume and fiber for very few calories, so your plate looks big and you feel full.

How to do it

  1. Buy 4 different bags: broccoli, spinach, stir-fry mix, cauliflower rice.
  2. Microwave a cup while your main food cooks.
  3. Stir it into whatever you are already eating.
  4. Restock when you get down to 2 bags.

Pro move: Roast frozen broccoli straight from the bag at high heat with a little oil and salt. It gets crispy edges, not mushy.

#033ShoppingQuick wins

The 5-Second Protein Test

One tiny math trick tells you if a food is working for you or against you.

Flip any package and find two numbers: calories and protein grams. Ask: does it have about 10 grams of protein for every 100 calories? If yes, it is a lean protein star. If it has less than 5 grams per 100, it is a snack pretending to be healthy.

Why it works

Protein keeps you full longer and helps you keep muscle while you lose fat. Many 'protein' bars and snacks are really just sweets with a little protein added. This test cuts through the marketing on the front of the box in seconds.

How to do it

  1. Look at calories per serving.
  2. Look at protein grams per serving.
  3. Move the decimal: 200 calories means you want about 20g protein.
  4. Keep the winners, put the pretenders back.

Pro move: Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, egg whites, tuna and chicken breast all pass easily. Most granola bars fail badly.

#034KitchenHungerQuick wins

The Ready Protein Rule

If protein takes 30 minutes, you will grab chips. Make it take 30 seconds.

Always have 3 kinds of protein in the fridge that need zero cooking. Think rotisserie chicken, hard boiled eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, canned tuna, smoked salmon or pre-cooked shrimp.

Why it works

Most people do not overeat because they love junk. They overeat because junk is faster. When protein is just as fast, you pick it more often, and it fills you up so the snacking stops.

How to do it

  1. Buy a rotisserie chicken and shred it the same day into a container.
  2. Boil 6 to 8 eggs at once and keep them peeled.
  3. Stock 2 tubs of Greek yogurt or cottage cheese.
  4. Put all of it at eye level at the front of the fridge.

Pro move: Pull the chicken while it is still warm. It comes off the bone in 3 minutes instead of 15.

#035KitchenMaintenance

Components, Not Meals

Meal prep fails because you get bored. Prep parts, not plates.

Instead of 5 identical boxes of chicken and rice, prep separate parts: one protein, one carb, two veg, and one sauce. Each day you mix them in a new way. Bowl on Monday, wrap on Tuesday, salad on Wednesday.

Why it works

Eating the same exact meal five days in a row is why most meal prep ends up in the bin by Thursday. Components give you variety with the same hour of work. Variety keeps you on track.

How to do it

  1. Cook one big protein, like chicken thighs or ground turkey.
  2. Cook one carb, like rice, potatoes or pasta.
  3. Roast two trays of veg.
  4. Make one sauce and store everything in separate boxes.

Pro move: Change just the sauce and spice each day and it feels like a totally new meal.

#036KitchenMaintenanceShopping

The Default Dinner Rotation

Decision fatigue is why you order takeout. Remove the decision.

Pick 5 easy, lean dinners you already like. Give each one a day of the week. That is your default. You can always change it, but if you are tired, the default wins.

Why it works

At the end of a long day your brain is worn out, and the easiest choice wins. When you have no plan, the easiest choice is delivery. A default dinner makes the healthy choice the easy choice.

How to do it

  1. Write down 5 dinners that take under 20 minutes.
  2. Assign each to a weekday, like Taco Tuesday.
  3. Build your grocery list from those 5 meals every week.
  4. Leave the weekend free and flexible.

Pro move: Stick the list on the fridge. When someone asks what is for dinner, the fridge answers.

#037KitchenQuick wins

The 3-Ingredient Protein Plate

You do not need a recipe. You need a protein, a veg and a flavor bomb.

Build fast meals from just three things: a lean protein, a vegetable, and one strong flavor. Examples: shrimp + frozen stir-fry veg + teriyaki. Eggs + spinach + salsa. Chicken + bagged salad + pesto.

Why it works

Complex recipes feel like work, so you skip them. Three items is simple enough to do on your worst day. Protein plus veg gives you fullness and fiber, and the flavor bomb makes it feel like real food, not diet food.

How to do it

  1. Choose a protein from your fridge.
  2. Grab a veg from the freezer or a bagged salad.
  3. Add one strong flavor: salsa, pesto, curry paste, hot sauce or everything seasoning.
  4. Cook or heat in one pan and eat.

Pro move: Cottage cheese + everything bagel seasoning + sliced cucumber is a 2-minute lunch that tastes like a bagel.

#038CravingsKitchenShopping

The Portion Pack Sunday

Never eat straight from the big bag again. Future you will say thank you.

When you get home from the store, split big bags of snacks into single portions right away. Nuts, crackers, popcorn, cheese, trail mix. Use small bags or boxes.

Why it works

When you eat from a big bag, you have no stop sign. You keep going until the bag feels 'done'. A small pack gives you a natural end point, so you enjoy your snack and stop without thinking about it.

How to do it

  1. Buy a box of small zip bags or mini containers.
  2. Read the serving size on the package.
  3. Split the whole bag into single servings as soon as you unpack.
  4. Put the packs in a basket so grabbing one is easy.

Pro move: Make the portion packs for your favorite treats too. It is not about banning them, it is about giving them a clear finish line.

#039KitchenMaintenance

The Big Batch Hour

One hour of cooking on Sunday saves you from ten bad decisions during the week.

Pick one hour a week to cook in bulk. Run the oven, the stove and the rice cooker at the same time. Make enough protein, carbs and veg for 3 to 4 days.

Why it works

Cooking every single day is where most people give up. Doing it all at once uses the same heat and the same cleanup for many meals. When food is ready, you eat it instead of ordering.

How to do it

  1. Put 2 trays of veg and a tray of chicken in the oven together.
  2. Cook a big pot of rice or potatoes on the stove.
  3. While it cooks, wash and chop fruit for the week.
  4. Cool everything and pack into clear boxes.

Pro move: Use clear containers. If you can see the food, you remember to eat it.

#040KitchenCravings

The Flavor Cheat Shelf

Lean food is not boring. You are just missing the right shelf in your fridge.

Create a shelf of low-calorie flavor boosters: hot sauce, mustard, salsa, pickles, lemon, garlic, vinegar, soy sauce, spice mixes, and plain Greek yogurt for creamy sauces. Use these first, and use creamy, oily dressings as a small extra.

Why it works

Most people quit healthy eating because the food tastes flat. Strong flavors like acid, heat and salt make food exciting without adding many calories. Butter, mayo and creamy dressings are not bad, but they add up fast when you pour freely.

How to do it

  1. Buy 3 new flavor boosters this week, like chili crisp, smoked paprika and a good salsa.
  2. Mix Greek yogurt with garlic, lemon and salt for a creamy dip.
  3. Squeeze lemon or lime on every plate before adding more salt.
  4. Measure oil with a spoon instead of pouring from the bottle.

Pro move: A spray bottle of olive oil gives you crispy roasted veg with a fraction of the oil.

Myth vs. Truth

Fresh vegetables are always healthier than frozen ones.

Frozen vegetables are usually picked ripe and frozen within hours, so they keep their nutrients well. Fresh veg can lose some nutrients while it sits in trucks and fridges. The best vegetable is the one you actually eat, and frozen ones never rot in your drawer.

Tonight's Try-This

Open your fridge and freezer and count your zero-cook proteins and bags of frozen veg. If you have fewer than 3 of each, write them at the top of your next grocery list.

Journal prompts

Which food in my kitchen do I overeat most, and could I portion it or stop buying it for now?

What 5 dinners could become my easy default rotation?

When do I usually order takeout, and what ready food would stop that?

“Your kitchen is louder than your willpower. Make it say the right things.”

— The Skinny Laws
↑ ContentsNext Law →
Law 08 of 12 🥤

The Drink Laws

Stop drinking calories your body never notices

“Your stomach counts food. It barely counts drinks. So chew your calories.”

Here is the sneaky part about drinks. You can sip a lot of calories and still feel just as hungry as before. Your body does not register liquid the same way it registers food you chew.

That means your latte, your juice, your smoothie and your weekend wine might be quietly adding up to a whole extra meal. And you still eat dinner on top of it.

This chapter is not about banning your favorite drinks. It is about knowing where the hidden calories hide, swapping smart, and building drink rituals that actually help you stay lean.

In this Law: The Coffee Order AuditChew Your FruitThe Protein CoffeeThe Bubbles RitualThe Tall Thin GlassThe Alcohol Triple ThreatThe Mocktail UpgradeElectrolytes, Not Sports DrinksThe Closing TeaThe Water Anchor
#041DrinksQuick winsEating out

The Coffee Order Audit

Your daily coffee might have more sugar than a donut. Let's fix that without losing the joy.

Look up the nutrition info for your usual coffee order today. Then change just one thing: fewer syrup pumps, a smaller size, or milk instead of cream. Keep the ritual, shrink the calories.

Why it works

Big café drinks with syrups, whipped cream and sweet creamers can have as many calories as a meal. But because you drink them, they do not fill you up. One small change repeated every day adds up to a big difference over a month.

How to do it

  1. Find your exact order on the café app or website and check the calories.
  2. Cut the syrup pumps in half. Most drinks have 3 to 6 pumps.
  3. Swap whipped cream for a sprinkle of cinnamon or cocoa.
  4. Size down one step and see if you even notice.

Pro move: Ask for 'half sweet' or '1 pump'. Most people cannot taste the difference after a week.

#042DrinksHunger

Chew Your Fruit

The same fruit fills you up way more when you eat it than when you drink it.

Eat whole fruit instead of drinking juice. If you love smoothies, make them thick enough to eat with a spoon, and add protein. Treat juice like a treat, not a health drink.

Why it works

A Penn State study by Barbara Rolls found people who ate a whole apple before lunch ate less at the meal than people who had applesauce or apple juice with the same calories. Chewing takes time and whole fruit keeps its fiber, which helps you feel full. Juice removes most of the fiber and goes down in seconds.

How to do it

  1. Swap your morning juice for a piece of whole fruit.
  2. If you make a smoothie, add Greek yogurt or protein powder and use less liquid.
  3. Pour it into a bowl and eat it with a spoon, with toppings you can chew.
  4. If you drink juice, use a small glass and have it with food.

Pro move: A smoothie bowl you chew feels like a meal. The same smoothie in a straw feels like nothing.

#043DrinksHungerQuick wins

The Protein Coffee

Turn your morning coffee into a drink that actually keeps you full until lunch.

Make your coffee with a scoop of protein powder or a ready-to-drink protein shake instead of creamer. Iced or hot, you get creamy and sweet with a big hit of protein.

Why it works

Protein is the most filling thing you can eat. Most people eat very little of it at breakfast. Adding it to a habit you already have (coffee) is the easiest way to get more of it without changing your routine.

How to do it

  1. Pour a vanilla or caramel protein shake over ice.
  2. Add a shot of espresso or cold brew on top.
  3. For hot coffee, whisk protein powder with a little cold milk first, then add the hot coffee so it does not clump.
  4. Taste and adjust. Add cinnamon if you want more flavor.

Pro move: A small milk frother makes protein powder silky smooth in 10 seconds.

#044DrinksCravings

The Bubbles Ritual

Your soda habit is really a fizz habit. Keep the fizz, drop the sugar.

Replace sugary soda with sparkling water that you make feel special. Use a nice glass, lots of ice, and real fruit or herbs. Have it at the times you usually reach for soda or a snack.

Why it works

A lot of soda drinking is about the feeling: cold, fizzy, a little treat. Sparkling water gives you the same feeling. Making it look pretty tells your brain this is a treat, not a punishment.

How to do it

  1. Buy a few flavors of unsweetened sparkling water.
  2. Fill a nice glass with ice.
  3. Add a squeeze of lime, a few berries, cucumber slices or fresh mint.
  4. Drink it at your usual soda time or when you want an afternoon snack.

Pro move: Add a splash of tart cherry or cranberry juice for color and flavor with very few calories.

#045DrinksKitchenQuick wins

The Tall Thin Glass

Change the glass and you change how much you pour, without even trying.

For any drink with calories, like juice, wine or soda, use a tall thin glass instead of a short wide one. Save the wide glasses for water.

Why it works

Our eyes are bad at judging volume. We look at how high the liquid goes, not how wide it is. So a wide glass tricks you into pouring more. A tall glass looks full with less.

How to do it

  1. Move the short wide glasses to the back of the cupboard.
  2. Put tall thin glasses in front.
  3. Pour wine into a smaller wine glass, not a huge one.
  4. Use wide glasses and jugs for water only.

Pro move: Stop pouring wine when the glass is at its widest point. That is roughly one serving in most glasses.

#046DrinksSocialEating out

The Alcohol Triple Threat

Alcohol hits your goals three times: at the bar, in your body, and tomorrow morning.

Know the three ways alcohol works against you. First, it lowers your guard so you eat more. Second, your body pauses fat burning while it clears the alcohol. Third, bad sleep after drinking makes you hungrier the next day. Plan for all three.

Why it works

Your body treats alcohol as a priority to clear out, so it burns that first and puts fat burning on hold. Alcohol also makes it easier to say yes to late-night food. And poor sleep can boost hunger and cravings the next day.

How to do it

  1. Decide how many drinks you will have before you go out.
  2. Eat a proper meal with protein before you drink.
  3. Have a glass of water between every drink.
  4. Plan a filling protein breakfast for the next morning so you are not hunting for greasy food.

Pro move: Order your first drink as a sparkling water with lime. You arrive calm and you are not drinking on an empty stomach.

#047DrinksSocial

The Mocktail Upgrade

You don't need a drink. You need something fancy in your hand.

When you want to join in without a lot of alcohol, order or make a real mocktail. Or try a spritz: a small pour of wine or spirit with lots of sparkling water and ice.

Why it works

At parties, a lot of drinking is about having something in your hand and feeling part of the fun. A great-looking mocktail or spritz gives you that feeling with much less alcohol and fewer calories.

How to do it

  1. Ask the bartender for soda water, lime, mint and a splash of bitters in a fancy glass.
  2. Make a wine spritz: half wine, half sparkling water, lots of ice.
  3. At home, mix sparkling water, crushed berries and fresh herbs in a nice glass.
  4. Alternate: one real drink, then one mocktail.

Pro move: Use a cocktail glass at home. Presentation makes a simple drink feel like an event.

#048DrinksMovement

Electrolytes, Not Sports Drinks

Unless you are running a marathon, that sports drink is basically soda.

For normal workouts and hot days, skip the sugary sports drinks. Use water with a sugar-free electrolyte packet or tablet, or just water and a salty snack after a long sweat.

Why it works

Sports drinks are made for long, hard exercise where your body needs quick sugar. For a normal gym session or walk, you do not need that sugar. Low-sugar electrolytes give you the salts without the extra calories.

How to do it

  1. Keep sugar-free electrolyte packets in your gym bag.
  2. Use plain water for workouts under an hour.
  3. Add electrolytes on very hot days or after a lot of sweating.
  4. Read the label: look for low or zero sugar.

Pro move: Sometimes a 'craving' in the afternoon is really thirst. Try a big glass of water with electrolytes first and see how you feel.

#049DrinksCravingsSleep

The Closing Tea

Give your kitchen a closing time with a warm cup that tells your brain 'we're done'.

After dinner, make a cup of herbal tea like peppermint, chamomile or rooibos. This is your signal that eating is finished for the day. Sip it slowly on the couch.

Why it works

Lots of evening snacking is habit, not hunger. A warm drink gives your hands and mouth something to do. Peppermint also leaves a fresh taste that makes food less tempting. Over time, the tea becomes a routine that says the kitchen is closed.

How to do it

  1. Buy 2 or 3 herbal teas you enjoy, like peppermint, chamomile or cinnamon.
  2. Make one right after dinner or when you clean up.
  3. Drink it in your relaxing spot, away from the kitchen.
  4. Brush your teeth after for a double 'done' signal.

Pro move: Choose caffeine-free teas at night so your sleep stays deep.

#050DrinksHungerQuick wins

The Water Anchor

Tie a glass of water to things you already do, and you'll never have to remember.

Instead of trying to 'drink more water', attach one glass of water to moments that already happen every day: waking up, each meal, and each coffee. Water first, then the thing.

Why it works

Vague goals like 'drink more' do not stick. Linking a new habit to an old one makes it automatic. A glass before meals also starts filling your stomach so you feel satisfied a little sooner.

How to do it

  1. Put a glass by your bed and drink it when you wake up.
  2. Drink a glass of water before every meal.
  3. Have a glass of water with every coffee.
  4. Keep a bottle on your desk in plain sight.

Pro move: Use a bottle with a straw. Most people drink more through a straw without noticing.

Myth vs. Truth

Smoothies and fresh juice are always a healthy choice.

Juice and many smoothies are full of fruit sugar with most of the fiber removed or broken down, and they go down fast. They are fine as a treat, but they do not fill you up like whole fruit. If you want a smoothie, add protein and eat it with a spoon.

Tonight's Try-This

Write down everything you drank today that was not water, plain coffee or plain tea. Pick one and plan a lighter swap for tomorrow.

Journal prompts

Which drink do I have almost every day without thinking about it?

When do I drink for comfort or habit, not thirst?

What drink ritual could make my evenings feel calm and finished?

“Sip slowly, chew your fruit, and let your drinks work for you.”

— The Skinny Laws
↑ ContentsNext Law →
Law 10 of 12 🎈

The De-Bloat Laws

Look leaner by tomorrow, the safe way

“Bloat is not fat. Treat it like weather: it passes faster when you stop panicking.”

Here is a secret that will save you so much stress: a lot of what you see in the mirror on a "fat day" is not fat at all. It is water, gas, and posture. And all three can change in hours, not weeks.

Fat takes time to lose. Bloat does not. That means you have real power over how you look and feel tomorrow morning, without starving, without weird teas, and without drinking less water.

This chapter gives you the safe, smart moves. No diuretics. No laxatives. No detox anything. Just the tricks that actually work with your body instead of against it.

In this Law: The Potassium PaybackDecode The WhooshThe Fiber StaircaseThe Air-Swallow AuditThe 10-Minute Digest StrollThe FODMAP PauseRibs Down, Instantly LeanerThe 24-Hour Event PlanThe Cycle CalendarSleep Off The Puff
#051BloatQuick winsKitchen

The Potassium Payback

Ate a salty dinner? Don't drink less water. Eat a banana and drink more.

After a salty meal, add a potassium-rich food and keep drinking water normally. Good picks are a banana, a baked potato, avocado, spinach, white beans, yogurt or coconut water. Then just let your body do the rest.

Why it works

Sodium makes your body hold extra water. Potassium helps your kidneys balance that sodium out, and drinking enough water tells your body it does not need to hoard. Cutting water does the opposite: your body holds on even tighter.

How to do it

  1. Next morning after a salty meal, eat one potassium food (banana, potato, avocado or spinach).
  2. Drink a big glass of water when you wake up and keep sipping all day.
  3. Go for a 20-minute walk to get things moving.
  4. Ignore the scale for 48 hours. It is water, not fat.

Pro move: Keep a bag of frozen spinach in the freezer. Throw a handful into eggs or a smoothie after takeout night.

#052BloatMindset

Decode The Whoosh

Stuck scale for 10 days, then suddenly down overnight? That's the whoosh. Here's why.

When you lose fat, your body sometimes holds water in its place for a while. So the scale freezes even though you are doing everything right. Then one day, it drops all at once. Your job is to know this so you never quit during the freeze.

Why it works

Your body stores carbs as glycogen, and each gram of glycogen is stored with roughly three grams of water. Stress hormones like cortisol can also make you hold water. Add salty meals, hard workouts and your cycle, and the scale can hide real fat loss for days. When stress drops and water releases, you see the whoosh.

How to do it

  1. When the scale stalls, check your waist with a tape measure instead.
  2. Keep your habits the same for 2 more weeks. Do not cut food harder.
  3. Add an extra hour of sleep and one relaxing thing (a walk, a bath) to lower stress.
  4. Write down the date of every stall so you can see the whoosh pattern over time.

Pro move: A big high-carb meal can actually trigger a whoosh a day or two later, because it can lower stress signals. Don't fear one normal pasta night.

#053BloatKitchen

The Fiber Staircase

Going from 10 to 35 grams of fiber overnight? Hello, balloon belly.

Fiber is amazing for staying lean, but your gut needs time to adjust. Add fiber slowly, like climbing stairs, not jumping off a building. Raise it a little each week and drink more water as you go.

Why it works

Your gut bacteria eat fiber and make gas while they do it. When you add a lot at once, the bacteria party gets loud and you bloat. Go slowly and your gut adapts, so you get all the fullness benefits without the puff.

How to do it

  1. This week, add just ONE fiber food per day (like a pear, a half cup of beans, or chia pudding).
  2. Next week, add a second one.
  3. Drink an extra glass of water for each fiber food you add.
  4. If you bloat, stay on the same step for another week before climbing.

Pro move: Cooked veggies are easier on the gut than big raw salads when you are just starting out.

#054BloatDrinksQuick wins

The Air-Swallow Audit

Your 'bloat' might literally be air you swallowed through a straw.

Some belly bloat is just swallowed air. Straws, chewing gum, fizzy drinks, eating fast and talking while chewing all push air into your stomach. Before an important day, cut these out.

Why it works

Every time you sip through a straw or chew gum, you swallow small bits of air. Fizzy drinks add gas directly. That air has to go somewhere, and often it sits in your belly and makes it look rounder. Sugar-free gum can also contain sugar alcohols like sorbitol that cause gas in some people.

How to do it

  1. Swap sparkling water for still water with lemon or mint for 2 days before an event.
  2. Drink straight from the glass, not a straw.
  3. Put the gum away and try a mint or brushing your teeth instead.
  4. Put your fork down between bites so you swallow less air.

Pro move: Love bubbles? Pour sparkling water into a glass and let it sit 10 minutes. Less fizz, same fun.

#055BloatMovementQuick wins

The 10-Minute Digest Stroll

A short walk after eating does more for your belly than a sit-up ever will.

Walk for 10 to 15 minutes after your biggest meal. Slow and easy is fine. You do not need to sweat. Just move.

Why it works

Gentle movement helps food and gas move through your gut, so you feel less stuffed and puffy. Research on post-meal walking also shows it can lower the blood sugar spike after eating. That means fewer energy crashes and fewer cravings later.

How to do it

  1. Set a phone alarm for 5 minutes after dinner that says WALK.
  2. Walk around the block, the parking lot, or even your home.
  3. Take a family member or call a friend to make it fun.
  4. Do it for 7 days and notice how you feel at bedtime.

Pro move: No time? Even 2 to 5 minutes of walking or cleaning the kitchen after eating helps.

#056BloatKitchenSocial

The FODMAP Pause

Big event tomorrow? Beans, onion and garlic tonight might be the reason your dress feels tight.

FODMAPs are certain carbs found in foods like beans, lentils, onion, garlic, wheat, apples and some dairy. They are healthy, but they can cause a lot of gas in some people. The day before a big event, pick lower-gas options instead.

Why it works

Some carbs are not fully absorbed in your small intestine. They move to your large intestine, where bacteria ferment them and make gas. Researchers at Monash University in Australia created the low-FODMAP approach for people with sensitive guts. You don't need the full diet, just a smart swap before big days.

How to do it

  1. The day before an event, skip beans, lentils, onion, garlic and big apples.
  2. Eat simple meals: rice or potatoes, eggs, chicken or fish, carrots, zucchini, spinach, berries.
  3. Use chives or the green part of spring onions for flavor instead of onion and garlic.
  4. Go back to your normal healthy foods the day after.

Pro move: This is a short-term event trick, not a forever diet. If you get strong bloating often, talk to a doctor or dietitian.

#057BloatShapeQuick wins

Ribs Down, Instantly Leaner

Change one thing about how you stand and your waist looks smaller in 3 seconds.

Many people stand with their ribs flared out and their lower back arched. This pushes the belly forward. Pull your ribs down, stack them over your hips, and roll your shoulders back. You will look taller and flatter right away.

Why it works

When your ribs flare up, your belly muscles stretch and your stomach pops forward. Bringing the ribs down lets your deep core muscles do their job, which pulls your midsection in. Rolling the shoulders back opens your chest and makes your whole shape look longer.

How to do it

  1. Stand sideways to a mirror. Breathe out fully like you are fogging a window.
  2. Feel your ribs drop down toward your hips. Keep them there as you breathe in through your nose.
  3. Roll your shoulders up, back, and down. Think 'long neck'.
  4. Practice this every time you wash your hands so it becomes automatic.

Pro move: In photos, stand at a slight angle, put your weight on your back leg and do the ribs-down breath right before the click.

#058BloatSocialQuick wins

The 24-Hour Event Plan

Crash dieting before an event makes you look worse. Do this instead.

Starving the day before a big event makes you tired, cranky and often more bloated, because you overeat later. Instead, follow a calm, simple plan: normal meals, lower salt, lower gas, lots of water, sleep, and a walk.

Why it works

Skipping food raises stress hormones, which can make you hold water. Then when you finally eat, you often eat fast and a lot, which means more air and more bloat. Steady meals, less salt, and good sleep let your body release extra water naturally.

How to do it

  1. Day before: eat 3 normal meals with protein and easy-to-digest carbs like rice or potatoes. Keep salt and ultra-processed snacks low.
  2. Drink water all day and add one potassium food.
  3. Skip alcohol, fizzy drinks and gum. Take a 20-minute walk. Be in bed early.
  4. Event day: eat a normal breakfast, avoid new foods, and do the ribs-down posture.

Pro move: Plan your outfit the day before. Soft, stretchy fabric in a darker color is the easiest win of all.

#059BloatMindset

The Cycle Calendar

Up 3 pounds the week before your period? That's not fat. Stop punishing yourself for it.

Many women hold extra water in the days before their period. Track your cycle and your weight together so you know what is normal for you. Then you can ignore the fake gain and keep going.

Why it works

Hormone changes during your cycle can make your body hold more water and salt, and can slow digestion. This is normal and it usually goes away a few days after your period starts. It has nothing to do with fat gain.

How to do it

  1. Use a period app or a calendar and mark the first day of each period.
  2. Write your weight next to it for 2 to 3 months to find your pattern.
  3. In your 'puffy week', eat less salty takeout, add potassium foods and keep walking.
  4. Do not change your diet because of the number that week. Compare to the same week last month instead.

Pro move: If your bloating is painful or very strong, see a doctor. You deserve to feel good all month.

#060BloatSleep

Sleep Off The Puff

One bad night can make your face and belly look puffier. Sleep is your cheapest de-bloater.

Short sleep can make you look and feel puffy the next day. Aim for 7 to 9 hours. Also, finish your last big meal 2 to 3 hours before bed so your stomach is not working all night.

Why it works

Poor sleep raises stress hormones, which can increase water retention. It also makes you hungrier for salty and sugary food the next day, which adds even more bloat. Eating a huge meal right before bed can also cause reflux and a heavy, puffy feeling in the morning.

How to do it

  1. Set a 'kitchen closed' time 2 to 3 hours before bed.
  2. Put your phone on the other side of the room 30 minutes before sleep.
  3. Sleep with your head slightly raised if your face is puffy in the morning.
  4. Drink a glass of water when you wake up, before coffee.

Pro move: Puffy face in the morning? A cold splash of water and 5 minutes of walking help it go down faster.

Myth vs. Truth

Detox teas and water pills flush out fat and bloat.

They mostly make you lose water and can make you dehydrated, and some have laxative effects that are harmful. The weight comes right back when you drink and eat again. Real de-bloating comes from potassium, water, sleep, less swallowed air and walking.

Tonight's Try-This

After dinner tonight, take a 10-minute walk, drink a big glass of water, and put your phone away 30 minutes before bed. Check your belly in the mirror tomorrow morning.

Journal prompts

What foods or drinks made me feel most bloated this week?

Do my 'fat days' line up with salty meals, bad sleep, or my cycle?

How would I treat my body differently if I knew most bloat passes in a day or two?

“Bloat is weather, not a verdict. Drink water, go for a walk, let it pass.”

— The Skinny Laws

Bonus 3

Restaurant Cheat Sheet

What to order (and what to watch) at 8 kinds of places. No salads-only rule required.

Italian

Order: Grilled fish or chicken with veg; share a pasta as a side, not a main.

Watch out: Bread basket + creamy sauces.

Mexican

Order: Fajitas or a burrito bowl: double protein, salsa, lettuce, half rice.

Watch out: Chips before the meal, sour cream, cheese sauce.

Sushi

Order: Sashimi, edamame, miso soup, one roll.

Watch out: Tempura and 'crunchy' or mayo rolls.

Burger place

Order: Burger with lettuce wrap or open-faced, side salad or shared fries.

Watch out: Milkshakes and double sauce.

Chinese / Thai

Order: Steamed or stir-fried protein with veg; ask for sauce on the side.

Watch out: Fried rice, sweet and sour, anything 'crispy'.

Brunch

Order: Eggs any style, smoked salmon, side of fruit; share the pancakes.

Watch out: Bottomless mimosas + the pastry basket.

Coffee shop

Order: Latte with milk of choice, no syrup or 1 pump; protein box if hungry.

Watch out: Frappes and 'seasonal' drinks (often dessert in a cup).

Pizza night

Order: Thin crust, veg + chicken topping, big side salad first.

Watch out: Stuffed crust and garlic dips.

Safety & support

This guide is for healthy adults who want to get leaner in a kind, sustainable way. It is general education, not medical advice. Talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before big changes, especially if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, under 18, take medication, or have a health condition.

Being lean should make your life bigger, not smaller. If food, weight or your body is taking up most of your thoughts, if you feel out of control around food, or if you are cutting out meals or feel you have to "make up" for eating, please reach out for support. In the US you can contact the ANAD helpline (anad.org) or talk to your doctor. In the UK, contact Beat (beateatingdisorders.org.uk). You deserve help, and it works.

You made it to the end of the Vault. Here's the secret: the people who stay lean forever are not stricter than you. They just have better systems. You now have 120 of them.

Pick your favorites. Make them boring and automatic. Come back when life changes. And when someone asks what you're doing differently, you can just smile.

With love,
